replies.author: iatrik
replies.body:
Yes and no. Developers hate to do any kind of marketing. That part is true.

But the main difference is the volume of marketing required. If you sell a game once on steam, you only have to reach that one person. From there, the platform will start marketing the game „for you“ via the Friends list. 

On mobile, even if you could ask for the same price as on steam, you’d still lose that same marketing tool.  
But with the willingness of players to pay even less on mobile (and premium games having strong f2p competition), you have to convince players „harder“ to sell your game to one person for a reduced price.

And yes, if you want to sell a free game, you’re not developing anymore, but optimizing your money spend per user vs money gained per user.  
And when you want to try to „play that game“, you need to create a game, which can attract a huge volume of players.   
Let’s say you involve marketing and pay 0,10€ per User, while only gaining 0,15€ per User.   
That results into each player only generating 0,05€.

And getting your game to a point where this is a better strategy over steam, you want to make at least 10.000€ minimum.. meaning you need to be able to attract 200.000 players, which is not easy.

Selling your game to 1.000 players for 10€ is much more doable in comparison without having to spend any money on marketing. 

And that also allows you to have full creative freedom in your product at the same time without having to worry about any retention rates, Store conversation, monetization etc..

Making money on mobile is simply much harder on mobile, when you’re a small fish. But when you’re a juggernaut in the business, you can create a huge revenue. But I wouldn’t recommend it to small devs and teams.

Regards!

comments.author: iatrik
comments.body:
As someone who is trying his luck in mobile dev, let me tell you it’s simple not worth it for solo devs and/or small companies. Let’s say you want to make a small condensed premium experience. If you sell it on steam for 4-5€ and your game is good, it’s quite a good deal. If you try to sell it on mobile for 1-2€, you better have a „good argument“ why your game should cost that much (and not be free). You’re competing this so many free games, that players consider „free“ to be the norm. So selling a premium game on mobile is already much more difficult. 

Next, you might ask yourself: „But what about free with IAPs?“. And this is now exactly the core problem. First, when you want to be free with IAPs, you’re directly competing with all the other big players on the market. So the „starting point“ is already „off“. But let’s say you’re still trying to go for it, then you’ll quickly realize that your entire game loop/game design has to be built around the monetization strategy and maximizing player retention. You cannot „just“ create a 2-3 hour experience and „call it a day“. You have to create a design, that players can invest 100s of hours into, while making sure that there are reasons for players to spend money on it (to convert players into purchasers). And even if you get to make a game that can fulfill all of those requirements, you still have to worry about how players will keep spending money, after they already „have everything“. So you have to make sure there’s enough content coming into the game over time that players keep having reasons to spend money.

So if you want to take advantage of the mobile market, you have to be a live-service game. And making those is both hard and has a huge amount of competition.

But even if you tell yourself: „I don’t care as long as I make the same as on steam“, then you have to compare the numbers case by case.

If you go premium on steam vs premium on mobile, you’ll have to charge less on mobile for the same product, while selling way less units. So that already favored steam.

If you go premium on steam vs free on mobile, the difference in „doable“ because much more obvious.   
Let’s say you’re aiming at a premium price of 10€ on steam as a starting point. You sell one copy, you gain 10€. You only need one person to be interested in your game. Simple.

If you want to make 10€ on mobile, you have multiple multipliers to take into consideration. First, you’ll need to ask yourself „How many players do I need in the game, before they generate 10€?   
In my case I have a little game that generates around 0,10€ per player on average. That means I need to have 100 players to get to the same 10€ as one interested person on steam.   
That also makes marketing a bit more tricky. On steam, I only need one person, who’s interested in my game. So finding that one person is not that difficult in isolation. But finding 100 players, who’re interested enough to try your game is much more difficult in comparison. Especially on the Playstores.

But even then, you have an additional conversation mechanism that does not exist on steam: „Gameplay“.

On steam, you just need to make sure that the players is either engaged long enough to the point he can’t return the game anymore (or where the experience was „good enough“). That’s a very „low bar“. Refunding the game is an active decision you do afterwards, because you really disliked it.

On mobile, a player might enjoy the game, but still never spend any money at all. Your game is another conversation tunnel to the „actual shop“. So being „good enough“ won’t turn players into customers. So the game itself has to meet a certain standard for you to even consider „buying it“.  
And this entire step you completely avoid by selling a premium game on steam. 

So there are a lot of conversation steps involved in the process. 

But here is another thing. If you want to „stand out“, you want to cater to a specific niche or do something „special“. Otherwise, you have to aim for casual appeal, which means directly competing with giants again. Sounds simple, but that also means that your overall pool of players, who will enjoy your game, is highly limited.  
So going for a strategy that converts a potential player pool of 10.000 players into a maximum income of 1000€ (on mobile assuming 0,1€/player) vs 100.000€ (on steam assuming 10€ price) games the decision very easy.

Ah, and last but not least: Money on steam is not the same as money on mobile. On steam, you will have people trade cs2 skins, trading cards etc. A lot of players are able to just buy a game with money that they still have „flying around“ on their account. The money is already spend. You won’t see your actual bank account lose any money. It’s already gone. So making a purchase becomes a lot easier in comparison to mobile.

Long story short: „If my goal was to make money, I wouldn’t create a mobile game as an indie dev or small indie team“. 

Hope this helps a little bit.

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body:
As others have said, the mobile market is already flooded with low effort shovelware and big business gacha games. 

There's also a *massive* barrier to entry on mobile - It's not just "pay a small feel and dump your game on steam," you need to pay yearly licensing to become a Google Play Developer/Apple Developer, there are *extremely rigorous app reviews* before your app gets published on the store that are repeated every single new build, etc.

My employer develops iOS/Google Play apps and I have direct eyes on our submission pipeline.  The shit we've had builds rejected for has often been *ridiculously* petty minutiae, And that's with a full team of professional developers building these apps.

Those pipelines are simply anathema for the type of slopware that typically gets peddled in this sub (which is precisely the whole point of why they do it).

replies.author: logical_haze
replies.body:
It could be that our game was different enough to not get caught up in the race. If you're creating another match-game or anything too common, you're indeed competing with companies that have hundreds of millions of dollars in ad spend.

When we set out to create AI Game Master, we noticed the domain does not have high competition. I think that really helped us grow organically.

Our biggest acquisition channel for a while was store-organic-exposure (it's called Browse on AppStore and Explore on Android). I think the stores saw people downloading the game, leaving good reviews, playing a long time, and eventually making purchases - so they picked up on the organic signal and amplified it.

I've launched tens of apps in my life, mostly for clients (had an app dev house). Seeing money come in the first month to launch was a CRAZY signal. In 99% of the lanuches I've seen, you get a bunch of downloads on day 1 and 2, and pretty much zero after that, not to mention actual purchases.

So when people were paying for that very first version, we knew we were up to something.

And regarding copying - I've always preached to air your ideas. Everything will die in the drawer, you have to let things out if you want to give them a chance. And:  
1. Once your open with your ideas, you start getting real market feedback/validation, and then can pivot. Whereas an idea only in your head grows too much in the - probably - wrong directions.

2. You'll find no one steals ideas. Execution is the real moat, no one goes "oooh! I just heard someone working on something cool! let's throw everything I'm doing, and develop from scratch everything he did up till now, and then more so to gain advantage!"

  
Hope this helps! Good luck!

Try fast, if succeeds -> great!   
if not, try again
